title: Training-Free Adversarial Robustness in Computational MRI
claim: Attacks break cyclic measurement consistency; we exploit that inconsistency as a loss to iteratively correct the input without retraining.
layout: 2 stacked panels; a) attack propagation rows, b) mitigation loop with zoomed dashed inset
description: Two stacked panels with tinted backgrounds. Panel a (blue, 'Attack Propagation') shows two rows of knee MRI images and k-space data flowing left to right through green boxes labeled with the reconstruction network f(...; θ). The top row is clean and the bottom row is attacked, marked by a red '+ Attack' arrow. The attacked row gives noisy, distorted outputs. Panel b (peach, 'Attack Mitigation') shows a feedback loop. A perturbed input goes through two network passes, then yellow 'Correction' and 'Projection' boxes feed back to the input, with a circular-arrow icon. A dashed callout on the right zooms into the loop. It has a sampling-mask diagram (acquired, synthesized, skipped), a yellow argmin loss equation, and images that clean up from step 0 to step N. Eye goes first to the MRI images and the equation.
caption: Overview of the proposed mitigation strategy. a) If there is an adversarial attack, the k-space corresponding to the reconstructions of MRI data synthesized from previous DL model outputs will be disrupted. b) This idea is used to devise a novel loss function to find a "corrective" perturbation around the input that ensures cyclic measurement consistency.
abstract: Deep learning (DL) methods have become the state-of-the-art for reconstructing sub-sampled magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data. However, studies have shown that these methods are susceptible to small adversarial input perturbations, resulting in major distortions in the output images. Various strategies have been proposed to reduce the effects of these attacks, but they require retraining. In this work, we propose a novel approach for mitigating adversarial attacks on MRI reconstruction models without any retraining. Based on the idea of cyclic measurement consistency, we devise a novel mitigation objective that is minimized in a small ball around the attack input. Results show that our method substantially reduces the impact of adversarial perturbations across different datasets, attack types/strengths and PD-DL networks, and qualitatively and quantitatively outperforms conventional mitigation methods. We also introduce a practically relevant scenario for small adversarial perturbations that models impulse noise in raw data, which relates to herringbone artifacts, and show the applicability of our approach in this setting. Finally, we show our mitigation approach remains effective in two realistic extension scenarios: a blind setup, where the attack strength or algorithm is not known to the user; and an adaptive attack setup, where the attacker has full knowledge of the defense strategy.
